summaries.example: Imagine a doughnut. You can see and count its hole, even though the hole is not made of dough. You can put a finger through it, fill it with something, or move it by moving the doughnut. This makes the hole seem like a real thing, but it also raises a puzzle: what exactly is it made of?
summaries.summary: Holes seem ordinary in everyday speech. We can see them, count them, describe their size and shape, and explain events by mentioning them—for example, water spills because a bucket has a hole. Yet a hole does not seem to be made of matter. It depends on something around it, such as the material of a doughnut or a roof, but it is not the same as that material. Philosophers therefore ask whether holes are real entities or whether sentences about holes can be translated into sentences about material objects and their properties. The problem becomes harder when we ask how holes can be seen, how to tell when one hole has become another, and how to count holes that touch or have disconnected parts. Theories give different answers. Some eliminate holes from our basic picture of reality. Others identify them with regions of spacetime, parts or linings of their hosts, disturbances in objects, properties, or localized absences. A philosopher who treats holes as real immaterial things must explain why holes always depend on hosts, can be filled, share locations with their contents, and have parts. The debate shows how a familiar word can hide deep questions about what exists.
key_ideas: We talk about holes as if they were things: we count them, describe their shapes, and say they can cause events.
Holes seem unusual because they are not made of ordinary matter, even though they are found in material objects.
Philosophers disagree about whether holes really exist or whether talk about them can be replaced by talk about objects with openings.
Different theories describe holes as regions of spacetime, parts of objects, absences, properties, or genuine immaterial things.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about holes teaches us that everyday language is not always a simple guide to what exists. It also connects ordinary experiences—like looking through a doughnut or fixing a leaky bucket—to big questions about matter, space, perception, and parts and wholes.

important_terms.definition: The study of what kinds of things exist and what they are like.
The study of knowledge, including how we know and perceive things.
The material object around a hole, such as the dough around a doughnut’s opening.
Something that partly or completely occupies a hole, such as water in a bucket’s opening.
An explanation that avoids adding a new kind of thing when existing things may be enough.

questions_to_think_about: Is a hole a thing, or is it only a way to describe an object?
If you fill a hole with water, is the hole still there?
If you punch two nearby openings in a card, do you have two holes or one hole with two parts?

summaries.example: Suppose a card is punched once and then punched again right beside the first opening. One description says there are two holes because there are two perforations. Another says there is one disconnected hole with two parts. The choice depends on what counts as a hole’s identity and how holes can have parts. The card’s material cannot settle the issue by itself, since philosophers can imagine changing or replacing the host while the hole remains the same.
summaries.summary: The philosophical puzzle of holes begins with a tension. Ordinary thought treats holes as objects of reference: we count them, locate them, describe their shapes, and sometimes cite them in explanations, as when a hole in a roof helps explain a leak. Perception and cognition also seem able to identify and track holes much as they identify and track material objects. But holes appear immaterial. Each is associated with a material host, and it may contain a material guest, yet the hole itself seems to be made of nothing. This raises several problems. If perception depends on causal contact with material things, how can we perceive holes? What makes a hole the same hole when its host changes or its contents are removed? How should nearby perforations be counted, and can a hole be disconnected? What explanatory work do holes do if material and geometrical facts can provide matching explanations? Perception adds another complication: the region seen through a hole is often treated as background, while the hole itself nevertheless seems to have a recognizable shape. Philosophical theories respond in different ways. Eliminativists paraphrase hole-talk using claims about perforated objects. Other accounts identify holes with spacetime regions, qualified regions, hole-linings, negative parts, or disturbances dependent on a medium. Further views treat them as properties, ways things are, relational entities, localized absences, or negative facts. Realists may instead accept immaterial holes, but must explain their dependence on hosts, fillability, shared location with guests, mereological structure, and topological variety. The debate is a focused example of how metaphysics examines the ontology built into common sense.
key_ideas: Holes have strong roles in common sense: people perceive, track, count, and use them in causal explanations.
Their apparent immateriality creates problems for perception, identity, mereology, and their explanatory role.
A causal theory of perception may seem unable to explain seeing holes if only material things can cause perception; theories of causally effective absences offer another route.
Theories range from eliminating holes, to identifying them with spacetime regions or object-parts, to treating them as disturbances, properties, absences, negative facts, or immaterial particulars.

A realist theory must explain special features: holes depend on hosts, can be filled without necessarily being destroyed, can share a location with a guest, and can have parts and different topological forms.
The preferred theory may depend on broader views about parsimony, space, spacetime, and the commitments of ordinary language.
summaries.why_it_matters: Holes are a useful test case for deciding whether familiar language reveals reality or merely organizes experience. The issue brings together metaphysics, philosophy of perception, theories of space and time, and the study of parts and wholes. It also shows why a theory may be judged not only by whether it sounds intuitive, but by whether it explains identity, causation, perception, and ordinary statements without creating new problems.

important_terms.definition: The branch of metaphysics concerned with what exists and what kinds of entities there are.
The study of knowledge and its sources, including perception.
A particular entity located in space and time, such as a cookie or a hole, rather than an abstract entity such as a number.
The material object in which a hole occurs; the host surrounds or supports the hole without being identical to it on many views.
The study of part–whole relations, including whether a hole may have disconnected parts.
A theory that explains holes without treating them as additional entities, often by translating hole-sentences into claims about holed objects.
The view that holes are genuine entities but are not made of matter; they depend on material hosts.
A view that a hole is a localized absence or another way an object or region is, rather than an independent object.

questions_to_think_about: Can every statement about holes be replaced by a statement about a material object and its properties? What might be lost in doing so?
If a hole moves when its doughnut moves, is it the same hole, or a succession of related spacetime regions?
Does filling a hole destroy it, or merely place a guest inside it? What would each answer imply?
Should perceptual experience count as evidence that holes exist, even if perception is normally explained through causal interaction?
How might theories of holes change our understanding of other absences, such as shadows or empty spaces?

summaries.example: A bucket with a hole lets water escape. It is natural to say that the hole caused the spill. But someone could explain the same event by describing only the bucket’s material shape, the opening, gravity, and fluid behavior. This creates a choice: is the hole an extra thing that helps explain the event, or is “the bucket has a hole” a convenient way of describing material conditions?
summaries.summary: The entry asks whether holes should be counted among the things that exist. Common speech treats them much like objects: we say that a cheese has several holes, that a hole has a shape and location, or that a hole caused water to escape. Human perception also seems able to recognize and track holes. Still, holes are puzzling because they do not appear to be made of matter. They have a material host, and they may have something inside them, but the hole itself seems like an absence. This leads to questions about perception, identity, counting, and explanation. If a hole’s host is changed, or if its contents are removed, what makes it the same hole? If two nearby punctures are connected, are they one hole or two? And if physical science can explain a leak through the bucket’s material structure and the behavior of water, is mentioning a hole really necessary? Philosophers offer several families of answers. Eliminativist views treat hole-sentences as alternative descriptions of holed objects. Other views identify holes with regions of spacetime, special portions of spacetime, parts or linings of their hosts, or disturbances in a medium. Still others understand them as properties, relations, localized absences, or negative facts. A more straightforward realist view accepts immaterial holes, but then has to explain their dependence on hosts, their ability to be filled without simply disappearing, their shared location with guests, and their part-whole and topological structure. The best option may depend on wider commitments about parsimony and the nature of space and time.
key_ideas: Holes are important in everyday thinking because we can perceive, count, locate, and describe them.
They seem to have size, shape, and histories, but unlike ordinary objects they do not seem to be made of matter.
Philosophers question how holes can be perceived, identified through changes in their hosts or contents, and counted when their parts are connected or disconnected.
Some explanations remove holes from ontology; others reduce them to spacetime regions, parts of hosts, disturbances, properties, or absences.
A theory that accepts holes as real must explain why they depend on hosts, can be filled, can share a location with what fills them, and can have parts.
The debate illustrates how different ideas about reality can support different interpretations of ordinary language.
summaries.why_it_matters: A simple opening in a bucket can reveal difficult questions about existence. Studying holes helps us examine whether words in ordinary language name independent things, describe properties, or summarize physical arrangements. It also connects familiar experiences with larger philosophical issues about perception, causation, space, and the structure of reality.

important_terms.definition: The study of what exists and what basic kinds of things make up reality.
The study of knowledge and how we perceive or understand things.
The material thing around a hole, such as a bucket, roof, or piece of cheese.
Something inside a hole, such as water in a cavity; a hole may remain even when its guest is removed.
The study of how things have parts and how parts form wholes.
The view that holes are not additional objects and that hole-statements can be restated using facts about objects.
The view that holes are real but not material objects.
A theory that treats a hole as a region, property, absence, or other feature rather than an ordinary independent object.

questions_to_think_about: If the bucket stays the same but its hole is repaired, what changed: an object, a property, or a region?
When two punctures touch, what rules should determine whether there are one or two holes?
Can a hole be perceived if it is not a material object?
Is an explanation using holes better than an explanation using only material objects and their shapes?
Would a hole be able to exist without the object around it?
